title: Nucleic Acids
short: DNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides, each a sugar, a phosphate and a base. DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps use it to build proteins.
trouble: Students think DNA and RNA are made of different kinds of building blocks altogether. Both are nucleotide chains; they differ in the sugar, in one base (thymine or uracil) and in usually being double or single stranded.

blocks.html: The fourth kind of large molecule holds the instructions for the other three. Nucleic acids are polymers too, built by the same dehydration synthesis from Monomers and Polymers.
DNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogen base. DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps use it to build proteins.

blocks.cap: DNA and RNA side by side.

blocks.html: In the chain, the sugar of one nucleotide bonds to the phosphate of the next, making a sugar-phosphate backbone. The bases stick out to the side. In DNA, the bases of the two strands pair by hydrogen bonds: A with T, G with C. The information is in the order of the bases, the way the meaning of a word is in the order of its letters. You will see this in detail in The Structure of DNA.

blocks.title: Spot the molecule
blocks.q: A nucleic acid has ribose and contains the base U. Is it DNA or RNA?
steps: Ribose is RNA's sugar (DNA has deoxyribose).
Uracil (U) is found in RNA, not DNA.

blocks.title: Count the parts
blocks.q: A piece of double-stranded DNA is 40 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it have, and how many phosphate groups?
steps: Each base pair is two nucleotides, one on each strand: $40 \times 2 = 80$ nucleotides.
Every nucleotide has one phosphate: 80 phosphates.

blocks.html: Thinking DNA and RNA are made of entirely different building blocks. Both are chains of nucleotides with the same plan (sugar, phosphate, base) and three of the same four bases. They differ in three ways only: the sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), one base (thymine or uracil), and usually the number of strands (two or one).
